newsitem.title: USA: China's MFN status headed for renewal.
newsitem.headline: China's MFN status headed for renewal.

text.p: U.S. trade advocates feel confident that after an emotional debate in Congress China's trade privileges will be renewed for another year, but they are less sure about new legislation on trade negotiations.

President Bill Clinton is expected to tell Congress soon that he will renew China's Most Favoured Nation trade status for another year. It would be up to lawmakers to overturn the decision, and few Washington analysts believe opponents can muster the votes needed to overrule the president.

Business leaders have been rallying commercial forces across the country since January to lobby lawmakers for renewal of the preferential trade status, which is given almost every country in the world. Only a handful of countries are denied MFN.
"It will be an emotional, nasty debate, and then after everybody ... has vented their spleen, it will pass the House," said U.S. Chamber of Commerce international expert Willard Workman.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich said this year's decision would be closer than last year's 286-141 vote to back Clinton on MFN. Supporters of normal trade relations with China had hoped to end the annual ritual and pass legislation this year to grant permanent MFN.

But strong opposition from social conservatives and liberal labour groups who criticised China's human rights record, and a scandal involving allegations that Beijing tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions, made that unlikely.

China's MFN status is a high priority for the White House, along with legislation giving it authority to negotiate trade deals. But the administration has yet to send Congress the proposed legislation.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Republican from Texas, fired off a letter to the president last week warning him time was running out if they hoped to get the so-called "fast-track" trade negotiation legislation through Congress this year.

The White House is trying to decide whether to move ahead with a proposal in June, when the China MFN debate will be in full swing and lawmakers will be deep into the budget, or wait until September, trade sources said.

Waiting until autumn would mean final passage would be pushed off until next year. Administration officials say they want it in place by the time Clinton meets other hemispheric leaders in Santiago, Chile, next March to launch Free Trade Area of the Americas negotiations.

"Our sense is that fast track is on a very slow track and the administration has been delaying, delaying and delaying introducing legislation because they keep not having enough votes," said Thea Lee, international expert at the AFL-CIO.
That is fine from the union's point of view, because it lacks the support needed to include labour and environmental issues in the negotiating authority.

Republicans oppose allowing labour and environmental issues to be part of trade deals. But House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, a potential rival to Vice President Al Gore in the 2000 presidential campaign, and the second-ranking Democrat in the House, David Bonior of Michigan, oppose fast track without the inclusion of labour and environment issues.
"We would like to boost the number of Democrats who are going to stand with us on that issue," Lee said.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin acknowledged the trouble the administration faces on fast track. Congress would give up its right to amend trade agreements and be able to vote only for or against them.
Rubin told an investment group that getting fast track "is going to be very difficult and the odds clearly are not in our favour."
